entries.title: Production-grade LLMs and agents: a field guide
entries.summary: A maturity model for taking agents from an impressive demo to a system people can depend on — with a self-assessment and the map to a deep-dive on each layer.
entries.content:
[Since we opened The Heap to contributions, we’ve gotten a lot of really excellent pieces of technical writing. Some of those we’re bumping up to the main feed so more folks can read their great work. This is one of those articles, so let us know what you think in the comments.]

There’s a canyon between an agent that demos well and an agent you’d put in front of customers or money. Crossing it isn’t about a bigger model — it’s the boring machinery around the model: determinism, evaluation, calibrated confidence, layered guardrails, an audit trail, and observability. This post is the map and the maturity model. Each layer links to a focused deep-dive.

The one-paragraph thesis

LLMs are probabilistic; production demands guarantees. You get guarantees not by making the model deterministic (you can’t) but by shrinking the model’s job to the smallest decision that needs judgment, then wrapping that decision in deterministic machinery you can test, gate, audit, and observe. The model is one contained component in an otherwise ordinary, well-engineered system.

The maturity model

Levels you climb, each assuming the one below.

The level — What you have· The tell for gaps

  • 0 - Notebook — a prompt, a model, a happy-path demo · “it works on my examples”
  • 1 - Determinism— agents propose (never act); fixed graph per capability; model contained to one node; loops bounded · the agent can write business state; behavior depends on the path it wandered
  • 2 - Evaluation — evals as a CI gate; baselines for drift; shadow evals from prod · you change a prompt and hope; evals live in a notebook
  • 3 - Confidence — composed, calibrated confidence; auto-vs-human threshold; sampled judge · you act on raw model confidence; no abstention
  • 4 - Safety & governance — defense-in-depth guardrails; PII at the boundary; append-only audit ledger; scoped memory · one moderation filter; raw inputs in logs; mutable audit
  • 5 - Operability — observability of decisions; cost control; model routing + fallback; kill switch · you learn about quality/cost from the invoice and the customer
  • 6 - Production-grade build — the build itself is disciplined — an OS for your coding agents, parallel agents on a decision log · tribal knowledge; decisions re-litigated every few weeks

How to use it: find your weakest level and fix that, in order. Most teams are strong at 0 and wish for 5 — but determinism comes before evals, evals before trusting confidence, confidence before automating, safety before scaling, observability before sleeping at night.

A 90-second self-assessment

Tick what’s true today:

  • An agent can only propose; a separate component applies changes after approval.
  • Each capability is a fixed sequence of steps; the model is one of them.
  • A prompt/model change that regresses quality fails CI.
  • You compare each release to a baseline, not just a pass/fail floor.
  • Decisions carry a composed, calibrated confidence; low confidence routes to a human.
  • Guardrails are layered (input, output, PII, verify, judge) and fail closed.
  • Sensitive data is redacted/hashed at the boundary; the audit ledger is append-only.
  • You can see decisions, guardrail blocks, token cost, and override rate on a dashboard.
  • You can stop automated decisions in seconds without a deploy.
  • Your hard-won decisions are written in a log humans and agents read.

Fewer than half ticked → you’re earlier than the demo suggests. The series below is the path.

The series — deep-dive per layer

Level 1 · Determinism 1. Make your AI agents boring · 2. Anatomy of an agent request · 3. Structured output over free-form · 4. Bounded ReAct: the one place loops belong

Level 2 · Evaluation 5. Evals as a deployment gate · 6. Drift detection in production

Level 3 · Confidence 7. Building on confidence · 8. LLM-as-judge · 9. Human-in-the-loop UX

Level 4 · Safety & governance 10. Defense-in-depth guardrails · 11. PII at the boundary · 12. The append-only audit ledger · 13. A memory model for multi-tenant agents · 14. Seed vs runtime

Level 5 · Operability 15. Hexagonal architecture for AI · 16. Observability for LLM systems · 17. Cost control · 18. Model routing & fallback · 19. Kill switches & graceful degradation · 20. Identity for agents · 21. What infrastructure an agent platform actually needs · 22. Making an agent pipeline fast

Level 6 · The build itself 23. Running a build with parallel autonomous agents · 24. The decision log 25. An operating system for coding agents

The takeaway

You don’t reach production by trusting the model more; you reach it by containing it more — and building the testable, measurable, auditable, observable system around it. Climb the levels in order. Each post below is one rung.

Series: Running LLM systems in production.

A maturity model for taking agents from an impressive demo to a system people can depend on — with a self-assessment and the map to a deep-dive on each layer.

entries.title: AI says you’re right, formal methods say you’re wrong
entries.summary: Ryan is joined by Gabriela Moreira, CEO at Quint, about why formal specification languages like TLA+ are essential for catching system design flaws before writing code, how Quint brings developer-friendly syntax and executability to formal methods, and the ways trace validation and model-based testing can verify AI-generated code against real-world production data.
entries.content:
AI says you’re right, formal methods say you’re wrong

Ryan is joined by Gabriela Moreira, CEO at Quint, about why formal specification languages like TLA+ are essential for catching system design flaws before writing code, how Quint brings developer-friendly syntax and executability to formal methods, and the ways trace validation and model-based testing can verify AI-generated code against real-world production data.

Quint is an open-source, executable specification language and toolchain based on TLA+ that enables engineers to model, simulate, and verify system behaviors using an intuitive, programmer-friendly syntax.

entries.title: MCP standardized tools. Now we need the infrastructure around them.
entries.content:
MCP adoption happened extremely fast.

Developers can now connect models to repositories, databases, browsers, observability systems, internal APIs, and dozens of other tools through a shared protocol. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, VS Code, and a growing list of other clients all speak it. Vendor-hosted endpoints exist for GitHub, Linear, Notion, and many others. The Tier 1 SDKs are approaching half a billion downloads a month.

That is a real achievement. For years every AI application built its own tool-calling layer. MCP gave the ecosystem a common interface. Once a server exists, multiple agents can use it without custom glue. That alone is worth the effort.

But after building around MCP for coding agents, I started noticing something else. The protocol was becoming standardized faster than the infrastructure around it. Connecting a tool was becoming easy. Running that system reliably across real users, real credentials, and real work was not.

The protocol solved a specific problem: how can an AI model talk to tools through a common interface? The next set of problems is different. How do we make thousands of those interactions reliable, secure, efficient, observable, and straightforward to deploy?

The demo-to-production gap

The happy path looks simple. An agent talks to an MCP client, which talks to an MCP server, which calls a tool that talks to an API or database. In a demo, that is often all you need.

In production, the picture changes. You have multiple agents, multiple users, many MCP servers, credentials that must not leak, rate limits, permissions that differ by person or by task, failures, retries, logs, tool schemas that change, context constraints, and machines that are not identical. The mental model becomes something closer to agents and clients sitting in front of authentication, routing or gateways, then a set of MCP servers, then the actual systems those servers touch. Every one of those layers can fail independently.

A concrete example: an agent that reads documentation and fails once is annoying. An agent that creates cloud resources, writes database records, or opens pull requests and fails halfway through is a different problem. Partial work, inconsistent state, and the need for idempotency or compensation become real requirements. The protocol does not magically supply them.

Everyone is rebuilding the same plumbing

One pattern I kept seeing is infrastructure duplication. Developers and teams repeatedly build authentication, deployment, connection management, retries, logging, secret handling, health checks, access control, simple registries, caching, and rate limiting. The same pieces appear in different codebases because the protocol standardizes the message format, not the operational concerns around it.

This is not unique to MCP. Earlier infrastructure transitions followed a similar shape. Once physical servers became painful enough, cloud abstractions matured. Once every application reinvented authentication, identity platforms matured. MCP may be entering a stage where managing dozens of individual local servers, each with its own configuration and credentials, starts to feel like the old way of doing things. Whether the eventual abstractions live in agent runtimes, cloud platforms, gateways, or somewhere else is still open. The duplication is already visible.

Local MCP was the right starting point

Local servers over stdio are easy to understand, close to the user, and naturally connected to local files and processes. They were the perfect way to experiment. Local execution also avoids many of the authentication and multi-tenant problems that appear once the server moves onto the network.

Team-scale usage exposes the limits. Everyone needs installation and configuration. Versions drift. Credentials live on different machines. One developer’s server can break differently from another’s. Onboarding becomes repetitive. Observability is fragmented because each machine is its own island. Remote or hosted servers address some of those problems, but they introduce others: authentication that actually works across clients, latency, multi-tenancy, data handling, uptime, permissions, and questions of vendor dependence. Neither model is automatically superior. They solve different sets of constraints.

The July 2026 specification changes helped the remote case. Removing protocol-level sessions and the initialize handshake means a remote server can scale more like an ordinary HTTP service. That is useful progress. It does not remove the need for authentication, authorization, or operational discipline.

Context is becoming an infrastructure problem

Coding agents need repository context. Naively giving an agent the whole tree creates token cost, irrelevant information, distraction, higher latency, and sometimes worse reasoning. Bigger context windows do not eliminate the problem. The question shifts from “how much can the model hold?” to “which context deserves to be there?”

This is where a lot of my early work sat. Hexum.dev began in part around making repository context more efficient, so the agent saw the relevant structure instead of a raw dump of files. On a published 24-task benchmark using MBPP and HumanEval, the measured context sent to the model dropped from 220,393 tokens to 27,352 (an 87.6% reduction) while still passing all official tests. The methodology is public. The number is less important than the observation: once you start treating context selection as a deliberate step rather than a dump, other constraints appear.

Developers talk about this constantly now under the banner of context engineering. Progressive or dynamic tool discovery is one response to a related problem: loading every tool schema from every server into the context on every turn. Client best practices now recommend deferring full definitions and providing a search-style meta-tool. The same guidance explains why: progressive discovery can dramatically reduce tool-definition tokens and can improve selection accuracy by keeping the model focused on a smaller set of relevant tools. The pattern is not universal yet, but the pressure is clear.

Tool explosion and selection

There is a point where giving an agent 50, 100, or several hundred tools becomes harmful rather than helpful. Selection accuracy can drop. Context fills with schemas the model may never need. Name collisions and vague descriptions make the problem worse.

Should every tool definition always sit inside the active context? Or should tools themselves be retrieved dynamically? Both approaches exist in the wild today. Static registration is simple when the surface is small. Progressive discovery, semantic search over tool descriptions, and gateway-style routing that exposes a smaller set are all being tried. The protocol itself is moving in this direction through progressive discovery guidance and related work. What remains open is how much of the selection logic lives in the client, in a gateway, in the server, or in the model’s own tool-use training. Least privilege also matters here: an agent that can see every tool is an agent that can be tricked into calling ones it should not have access to.

Security becomes more serious as agents become autonomous

MCP security is not the same as ordinary API security. An agent can read untrusted text, interpret it as instructions, call tools, and mutate external state. That creates surfaces that look like prompt injection, confused-deputy problems, over-broad permissions, malicious or poisoned tool descriptions, secret leakage through arguments or results, and supply-chain risk from the servers themselves.

None of this means the protocol is inherently insecure. It means that once natural language can cause software to invoke real capabilities, the trust boundaries and permission model become critical. Least privilege, explicit approval for destructive actions, careful handling of tool results as untrusted input, and authentication that survives the full path from client to server to backend system all matter more than they do for a conventional API. A 2026 measurement study of 7,973 live remote MCP servers found that 40.55% exposed tools without authentication. That is a deployment problem, not a protocol problem, but it is the problem teams actually hit.

Reliability when agents start doing real work

A human using software notices an error and stops. An autonomous agent may continue. That changes the requirements around retries, idempotency, timeout behavior, partial failure, and validation of tool results. Observability becomes more important because you may need to reconstruct what the model believed, which context it saw, which tools it knew about, which one it selected, what arguments it generated, what the tool returned, and what it did next.

Standardized telemetry is starting to appear. OpenTelemetry’s GenAI semantic conventions include MCP-related spans and attributes. Work such as SEP-414 reserves space in _meta for W3C trace context so traces can cross the MCP boundary. The official Python SDK now emits OpenTelemetry spans by default. Whether this becomes the default way teams debug agent-tool systems is still early, but the demand is obvious once agents move past demos.

What building Hexum.dev taught me

At first I thought one of the main problems was context efficiency. Hexum.dev’s early work on shrinking repository context for coding agents reflected that. Once you optimize context, you run into tool selection. Once you expose tools, you run into deployment and configuration. Once tools are remote, you run into authentication and permissions. Once agents become more autonomous, reliability, security, and observability move to the front. The realization was that MCP is not merely a protocol problem. It is becoming an infrastructure category.

Hexum.dev today is a hosted remote MCP endpoint for coding agents. Its scope grew as we ran into adjacent problems around context handling, architecture checks, and controlling agent behavior. The agent still lives in the editor the developer already uses; Hexum.dev sits around specific parts of that workflow. Building it did not eliminate the surrounding problems. It made them concrete.

There is one lesson from building Hexum.dev that has nothing to do with protocols.

Most of building is uncertainty. Things fail, direction changes, and you spend a lot of time on ideas before anyone validates them. Having friends who listen, encourage you, and challenge you when needed matters more than founders often admit. Yuchen and Pranav have been two of those people for me. They are not building Hexum with me, but they have listened to countless ideas and made the uncertain stretches easier to keep moving through.

MCP infrastructure might become its own layer

A possible future stack looks something like this: models and agents at the top, agent runtimes and MCP clients beneath them, then an infrastructure layer that handles routing, authentication, permissions, context management, tool discovery, caching, observability, policy, and reliability, then the MCP servers themselves, then the databases, APIs, code, and SaaS systems those servers touch.

This is a hypothesis, not a certainty. Some of those capabilities may end up inside model providers, inside agent runtimes, inside cloud platforms, inside gateways, or inside individual MCP servers. The boundary is not fixed. The interesting part is that the protocol’s success is forcing the question. Once tool interoperability is taken for granted, the remaining work is everything required to make that interoperability production-grade.

The protocol was the start

MCP’s biggest achievement may be that developers are beginning to take tool interoperability for granted. That is what successful standards eventually do. They make a previously hard problem feel ordinary.

Standards rarely eliminate infrastructure. They move the infrastructure problem somewhere else. HTTP standardized how systems communicate, but we still built CDNs, load balancers, API gateways, observability platforms, identity systems, and cloud infrastructure around it. MCP may follow a similar path. The protocol gave agents a common language for tools. Now we have to build everything required to make that language reliable at scale.

The interface is no longer the hardest part. The systems around it are.

entries.title: Why your platform team shouldn't build an AI context layer (even though they probably could)
entries.summary: Most engineering teams capable of building an internal AI knowledge system think they should. But six months later, it's a platform team's full-time job. Building an in-house AI context layer costs more money and energy than you think.
entries.content:
Most engineering teams capable of building an internal AI knowledge system think they should. Stand up a vector database, wire in a few connectors, point a RAG pipeline at your docs—easy, right?

Six months later, it's a platform team's full-time job.

That's not because anyone underestimated the database work, but because "vector database" and "governed knowledge pipeline" are two different classes of problem. One is a weekend project, but the other is a trust, compliance, and continuous-maintenance challenge that compounds with every new source, every stale doc, and every agent you plug in.

A production-grade pipeline breaks into five stages:

The stage that looks easiest might be the hardest

Every stage above looks tractable on its own. You might be thinking that a strong team could build all five, and you’re probably right. The trap lies in underestimating what it costs to keep that pipeline up and running. None of these are one-and-done costs; they compound with the sophistication of your AI stack.

Stage What looks easy What it actually takes to keep working
Capture Connect to a few tools, pull in the data Someone has to keep every connection alive as each tool updates itself, leaving users to manually reconnect and adjust permissions every time an auto-update happens. Plus, they have to make sure the same document isn't showing up three different ways
Deliver Hook the AI up to the database Making sure every tool and AI agent in the company is always working from the same up-to-date, trustworthy answer
Govern Turn on some access controls The permissions, approval rules, and audit history that security and compliance teams will actually ask for
Organize Sort content by team Logic that knows when a piece of knowledge has earned its way from one person's notes to the whole company's source of truth (without anyone filing it by hand)
Validate Let people upvote or flag what's useful A system for deciding what to trust automatically, plus a process for looping in the right expert when the stakes rise

Capture: Because raw documents aren't enough

Writing a connector isn't the hard part. That’s keeping it current as vendor APIs evolve. And bear in mind that even a perfect connector only gets you a copy of the source. After all, agents can't skim content the way humans can: if you feed one a raw Slack thread, it will often retrieve the right document but the wrong section.

That's why capture needs to produce something more durable than a stored copy: a knowledge node, or a living record that carries the substance of what's known, where it came from, who owns it, and how much to trust it. If the source tool disappears tomorrow, the knowledge stays put.

Validate: Where trust actually gets built

This is the layer most build-it-yourself pipelines skip, but it's the one that matters most. Treating all captured content as equally trustworthy is the single biggest mistake in enterprise AI context layers. Some knowledge is authoritative; some is a reversed decision nobody labeled accordingly. Without a way to tell the difference, agents will surface both with equal confidence.

Validation works in two modes: implicit trust, which is automatic, and explicit trust, which is a human-in-the-loop fallback for when the stakes are too high for guesswork.

Every knowledge node carries a trust score built from multiple signals: factors like authorship, usage, recency, source, and whether it conflicts with other knowledge. Most content earns trust automatically, in the form of a merged PR from a principal engineer or a finalized policy with a named owner.

Trust also decays, however. A node that was accurate six months ago may not be today, so a node that falls below a confidence threshold surfaces a lightweight one-tap revalidation request to its owner.

Implicit vs. explicit trust

Implicit trust Implicit trust
Default or fallback? Default: no human needed Fallback: used when the cost of being wrong is high
Design goal Handle as much as possible automatically Drive the number of human interruptions toward zero over time
What it looks like A trust label and signal on every search response A one-tap prompt, in-context correction, or knowledge-inbox review
Who's involved The system alone The right owner, prompted at the point of decay or conflict

The health metric that matters here is, How many times did we interrupt a human today? Every interruption is a signal that the automatic layer isn't working well enough yet.

Organize: Knowledge in the right spaces

Not all knowledge merits the same audience. A decision made by one engineer about their own service, for instance, shouldn't carry the same weight—or reach the same people—as a company-wide architectural commitment. We solve the problem of organization with scopes solves this by giving knowledge context, defined by what information is in scope and who can work within that scope. This organization is auto-populated rather than manually filed, so knowledge naturally settles into the right spaces instead of pooling into one undifferentiated room that everyone has to wade through.

Knowledge starts personal and private by default: the context a developer keeps re-explaining to their AI tools every session about who should and shouldn’t have access is instead inherited through scopes. Scopes organize knowledge into the relevant context and apply those inherited permissions from ingestion when retrieving and composing an answer. Agents inherit the same permission boundary as a human operating in that same context, so a developer's personal knowledge never leaks to their team without their permission, and a team's knowledge never leaks to the wider org unless someone explicitly chooses to share it.

Govern: The control surface enterprise buyers actually need

Governance for AI has to work as an automated system that plugs into the tools enterprise IT and security teams already use. Buyers signing off on a company-wide AI rollout have their own requirements: they need to set permissions in bulk rather than one person at a time, they need proof of who accessed what to feed into their existing security monitoring, and they need visibility into how the system is being used without having to log into yet another dashboard.

Govern has to satisfy both audiences at once: the person browsing a settings page and the automated systems checking in behind the scenes.

As agents take on more consequential work like answering support queries or informing product decisions, the ability to trace any AI output back to a specific piece of validated content, approved by a named reviewer on a specific date, becomes a compliance requirement instead of a nice-to-have.

Deliver: Getting trusted knowledge to where work happens

Validated, organized, governed knowledge that nobody encounters might as well be locked in a filing cabinet. Delivery has two modes: explicit, where a user asks and gets the best available answer with a trust score and provenance trail attached, and proactive, where the system surfaces relevant knowledge before anyone asks (for instance, an engineer opens a new service and the system already knows a similar team hit this exact bottleneck six months ago).

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) makes this composable instead of bespoke. You have one standardized interface instead of every agent building its own retrieval integration, so you’re constantly querying the current, validated state of the graph rather than a stale snapshot.

So, build or buy?

The answer to that question hinges on what your engineering org is actually for. If knowledge infrastructure is your competitive advantage, then owning that pipeline is a legitimate play. But for most product companies and developer platforms, the pipeline just needs to work reliably without consuming engineering cycles that should go toward what customers actually pay for.

Connector maintenance, trust-model tuning, SME workflows that scale with headcount, governance requirements that show up the moment an auditor asks for a trail…as we mentioned, none of these are one-time expenditures, and they compound as your AI stack gets more sophisticated. The build vs. buy decision for knowledge infrastructure boils down to a question of organizational focus. Building a vector database is easily achievable. Building a governed, trusted knowledge pipeline? Not so much.

The Stack Internal platform is built to absorb those costs: capture that runs on a stable connector framework instead of a fleet of bespoke integrations, validation that earns trust automatically before it ever asks a human, organization that scopes knowledge correctly without manual filing, governance with audit and guardrails as foundation, and delivery that’s MCP-native by default.

Interested in seeing how Stack Internal handles the full pipeline? Learn more about Stack Internal here.

entries.title: Your next job doesn’t have a title yet: Emerging role skills Q&A with Cory Hymel of Andela
entries.summary: While the whispers say that everyone is becoming a generalist, that's not where headcount is going.
entries.content:
There’s been plenty of chatter about AI’s effect on jobs. Will everyone get laid off to train AI? Will every developer become a super generalist? Are there new roles rising from the ashes? But Cory Hymel, head of research at Andela, wanted numbers behind that chatter. He and his team looked at nearly 50,000 job postings to find the skills and roles that are emerging before the industry has properly given them titles. I spoke with him to find out what that research says about the new developer skillsets that land permanent roles.

—---------------------------------------

Q: You did this research on how skills shift and change in job titles. Could you give an intro to this to the project?

A: At Andela, our general approach and methodology to the market is that job titles and resumes are the best worst thing that we have out in the world right now. We're obsessed with understanding very fine-grained skills of what people are able to do.

That's premise number one. Premise number two was that we hear very commonly "Oh, AI is changing jobs. Oh, AI's gonna get rid of jobs," or, "AI is, gonna create new jobs." But it's all very anecdotal and not very data-driven. We looked at it and said, "Is there a way that we can actually go in and put some numbers and some rigor to actually understand what's going on behind the curtains with all of these jobs?" We've got a internal skill taxonomy and ontology that we use that grounds all of this and is the base of the research and data structure that goes in.

But for us, it's really important because the other big side of our business is around learning and upskilling. So how can we provide our customers information around where the industry is heading. Here's some skills that people should be learning that we're seeing become more common. These are the roles. Some of these might fall in between two.

While you might say, "Front-end engineers need to go learn this," actually you probably should pull in product managers as well.I think job titles have always lagged the work, but especially now it's getting worse and worse.

Q: So it's not necessarily about job titles changing, but more about new skills being applied to existing job titles and mid-range roles appearing. I think you talked about DevSecOps as an example of a bleed role.

A: Exactly. What I'm seeing in the news pretty frequently is that this pervasive narrative that AI's gonna make everyone generalist, and it's just turning these jobs into gray jobs where skills can bleed all over.

And what the data shows is that isn't true. There are very niche skill bundles that are either forming as these net new roles that no one's talked about yet or the underlying skills within historical roles are starting to change.

From the labor market or the hiring side, it's, one, happening so quick that people can't keep up with it. Or two enterprises don't really know what skills people should be learning, so they just give up this generalist title of AI engineer. It's like, what what does that mean? There's 100 different flavors of what that could be. But for them it's just easier to say "Oh, we need someone that does AI."

Q: At re:Invent last year, Amazon's CTO, Werner Vogels, talked about the T-shaped developer, where you have a deep focus but a broad base of understanding. Does your data reflect that? Or are you seeing a more specific concentration of these skill bundles?

A: I've gotten that question a few times, and transparently, I've not followed up with it as much as I probably should have. Because you have the T shape and you have the I shape, and I think there's a star shape. I've gotten questions about a few different ones, but from what we're seeing, I think that probably the T shape does typically follow the pattern in the data. But I don't have a definitive answer on that yet.

Q: That's something I'd love to know because, anecdotally, I hear a lot of people talking about this broadening of what a fullstack developer is that's covering product design to SRE. I wonder if people are actually hiring roles for that or if that's just something that happens within organizations.

A: I don't know. We didn't see in the data this idea of a net generalist. But what we are seeing is that if you look at the typical flow of the software development life cycle, if you put roles down in some linear fashion of product manager and then front-end engineer, back end engineer, DevOps, and then QA, the bleed in between those roles are where we're starting to see the most common mix in skills.

So for instance: the front end product engineer. This might be like a like an F-shaped engineer. Meaning that like they lean to one side—they might have a background in front-end engineering, but now they're being asked to stretch into a product role to talk to customers to get feedback, to prioritize and backlog features, and so on.

We're seeing the same thing on the back-end and the DevOps side of back-end engineers now needing to know about deploying these models into production and think about scalability and stuff—that F goes in the other direction.

I need to think about my shapes a little more for this.

Q:That shape is interesting, though. The F shape one— with AI, now that you're able to touch the things that are closest to you, you can branch out, right? Back end engineers can start touching the database and stuff like that.

A: Even to some degree like merging over into prod, even into the front end side too.

Q:What are some of the the skill bundles that you saw in the research?

A: One of the ones our customers often describe but never label was this idea of an LLM application engineer. This is someone that's very versed in building products on top LLMs, whether it's OpenAI APIs or open weight models or Claude code. They know how to plug into the APIs, but they can also take the step beyond that, meaning that they know how to construct the harnesses.

They know and are familiar with things like evals, which when we talk to customers, they think about it as just a backend engineer. That's a very specific skill set. Your classical back-end engineer will not necessarily know about building agent eval harnesses or governance and guardrails. That one was super interesting and also showed up pretty prevalent in the data.

Another one that I've heard it a few times now, is that 2026 and 2027 is gonna be the year of the CFO. How to deal with consumption spending. Now you have new products that are all on these consumption models, which pass-through products. Not only that, but your developers are consuming these new kind of OpEx spends. A FinOps reliability engineer, someone that's able to think about project development and factoring the cost—not just of typical end-user consumption, like cloud consumption—but also developer tooling. When we're building our AI-native SDLC, people talk about financially responsible ways to do this. We hear a lot about how do we optimize our token spend and how do we reduce our token spend. An engineering role that's very keen to understand costs, like in these cases, we use cheaper or faster models with simpler processes, or we design these to have where you might need Fable or something else because it is highly complex,

The last one was this docs-as-code engineer.

We hear a lot about spec-driven development. It’s treated like something that should be pushed down directly on top of developers, when in reality, there is this new role where people that were doing classical technical writing or classical documentation are some of the best spec-driven engineers. They're the ones that construct the context better than developers can to feed into these new models, as well as set the context for long-term agentic development on these bigger code bases.

Q: The AI application engineer is an interesting one—I hear a lot from people that everybody should be building their own software factory. It seems like this is the thing you're expected to do as an individual engineer, no matter what, because everybody's going through an agent, everybody's doing evals on their own code. It's interesting to see that these skills are specialized in the data.

A: I think that's the big I think insight with all of this. It challenges the narrative and the status quo of, either one, everyone's just gonna be the expanded fullstack developer, or two, everyone's just a generalist and you can just do everything now. In reality, we are seeing statistically significant trends of specific skill groupings that are coming out in hiring and job data.

Q: Did you notice anything about job titles? Do job titles matter for these skill groupings?

A: In my opinion, job titles are important, especially in this context, because it gives enterprises a way to better describe the work that needs to get done. When you look at an enterprise and how a job gets created, specifically when it comes down to the job title, you've got the individual that's closest to the work. A lot of times they might be someone within the team.

But there's layers on top of it, right? It's gotta go to HR, and then to finance, and then procurement, and then eventually a recruiter. You get this chain of custody, and the work gets more ambiguous as it goes down that chain of custody, not only in the description, but the understanding of what the role should be. What I've seen is that the fallback to a generalist role becomes easier.

I hope that with these more specific job titles, from the person that's closest to the work all the way to the edge recruiter, they're able to accurately describe exactly what needs to get done. A better title for that is really important. Because one, it allows the hiring firm to be more specific, it reduces their time, they get better candidates. It puts them in a better place to succeed.

From the candidate side, imagine I've been a back-end engineer for the past 20 years and I now see a back-end engineering role. I'm just hitting apply because I just need to get a job, right? The odds of me ending up in a position where I won’t be successful is relatively high because the underlying skills and requirements and understanding could be vastly different.

I do think in this case it is it is important for these new titles to come along.

Q: In the research post you talked about talent debt. What is talent debt?

A: Talent debt accrues the same way that technical debt does. But the difference with talent debt is that the skill half-life is shrinking substantially. Back in the day, you could go and get a job as a Java engineer and work for 20 years doing Java programming and be okay. But now what we're seeing is that the pace of change is going so fast that the half-life of how long those skills stay relevant is shrinking substantially.

What you get is this skill compression, which then forms into talent debt. A lot of companies are experiencing it now where all of a sudden this race into AI, they look at what they have on the bench and say, "Oh my goodness, we've got nothing even close to what we have to do here."

They have two options then. One is either try to reskill who you have already. Upsides are that you get to keep the strong domain knowledge of the individuals within your team, understand strong system knowledge, and it's good to invest in your people.

The flip side is to try to hire it out. It's faster, but you don't have the domain knowledge, you have ramp time, and you have the the risk of putting the wrong butt in the wrong seat. All of that compounds into this concept of talent debt, which is very similar to technical debt.

Q: Developers have always had to keep learning on the job, right? Even if you're a Java engineer for 20 years, you're learning new frameworks, new features come out, new libraries. Is this acceleration a different sort of thing, where it's not just learning new things for Java, but learning a whole new thing every six months?

A: I think so. It's one thing to pick up a new framework, right? It's one thing to pick up a new programming language. I think a lot of developers are fine with that. The big difference now is that it's a fundamental bedrock shift of the way that you actually work.

That is the big, hard transition. Changing from procedural to object-oriented programming makes you really think structurally about how these things get built, what are ways to optimize and go faster. For a lot of people, that's a stiff change. If you've ever tried to switch between the two, doing C or something procedural into an object-oriented framework, you conceptually think about things much differently.

It's thinking conceptually differently, but at a much bigger scale of how you work as a person. For an engineer, it's going beyond and having to relearn syntax or language or frameworks or methodologies, but into a structural re-understanding how you put all of these new tools to work. How do I actually step back from the code, and how do I adjust in my mind what accountability is and give that to a virtual synthetic knowledge worker.

The engineers that are able to move in between it are ones that have substantial advantage. There’s an engineer working with me from our network making some updates to one of our platforms. He gave me a quote on the time because it was adding some leaderboards in, and I said, "We just need to add a leaderboard. You go give it to Claude Code. This should be an hour."

He was looking at it over four days, so I asked him, "Why does it take so long? Like coding tools are you using?" He uses Claude Code to understand it, but still hand codes everything to a large degree. He doesn't practice agentic development, mostly because he feels accountable for the code that he ships. “If something that I ship is wrong, then that's on me."

I have another developer that just gives it to Claude. If it works, if it passes the unit test and the acceptance test and the smoke test, then ship it to prod. Who cares.

It's interesting to see these different dynamics, but the other underlying one was that the developer that was very hesitant about using it has been using the tools for a while, but has a very small token budget. I think that there's like this fluency gap between those that can, developers that can afford to like fully embrace this new world and have the budget to burn the tokens to get the comfortability with it versus a large group of people that don't. That might be another area of study.

Q: You’re talking about scaling up and becoming comfortable with the tools, but I've heard a lot about AI affecting developer skills, de-skilling, growing lazier with cognitive offloading, people knowing less about the code., Like you said with the the one that's in YOLO mode—if it works, who cares how it works? Do you think AI will make the rescaling and the scaling up harder or easier?

A: I believe there's a lot of different answers to it. On one degree, AI will make upskilling a lot easier, right? You have a personalized tutor. It can explain things to you. I've seen good engineers ask Claude to quiz them on the code so that they get a firm understanding.

Is there gonna be skill degradation? For sure. I think that's one of the premises of any new technology that comes out. Gartner had this skill atrophy onion where you have your core skills that make you who you are. You've got skills that are unique to your domain that are not usually replaceable. Then you have this middle onion skill, which are these skills that are okay to atrophy. For a developer, that might be things like understanding the syntax. I don't necessarily need to know Go to write a Go program anymore. Is that an okay thing to let go? There are some skills in there, maybe general architectural setup that still trigger the sniff test of this doesn't seem just right.

Engineers that have been around for a while that are okay with letting some of these skills go and gaining these new ones are gonna be in extremely good position to accelerate forward. The people that I have concern about are individuals coming into the market now that haven't had time to develop that innate sniff test of when things are going awry and just blindly YOLO stuff. Upskilling and reskilling and skill atrophy or degradation is gonna be a problem in five, ten years when that gap forms.

Or maybe who cares? We weren't allowed to use calculators in school. Now everyone's got calculators, and we turned out fine.

Q: Nobody's coding in Assembly anymore, right? Doesn't matter.

A: Exactly.

Q: For folks who are a little antsy about the future of their jobs and their skills, does this data validate those fears?

A: I think there is a lot of noise about AI making everyone general. There is a lot of AI noise around AI changing jobs. But what we found is that there are new specific skill sets coming out becoming extremely important. People should understand where they fit. We've got another tool where you can put in your current role and we can show you the new role that it's morphing into.

Understanding where the trends are going and where, as an engineer, you can start to invest effort to prepare yourself will be really helpful for everyone.

entries.title: Why Your Sandbox Never Quite Matches Production (And Why That's Fine)
entries.summary: Sandbox testing works best when you stop chasing production parity. Learn what environment drift actually costs and which parts are worth fixing.
entries.content:
The sandbox has never matched production. Not yours, not anyone's. A configuration variable set differently. A database seed that skips the legacy record formats real users actually have. An upstream service that deployed a new response schema last Thursday and nobody updated the simulation. These are not edge cases - they show up in every environment, on every team, at every scale. The gap is structural. It comes with the territory. What changes when you accept that is where you put the maintenance work.

What Environment Drift Actually Is

Drift accumulates because production and the sandbox change on different schedules, with different triggers, and nobody coordinates the two deliberately enough.

Production evolves constantly. Application deployments, infrastructure updates, upstream service API changes, database schema migrations, third-party integration updates - each of these moves production forward in some dimension. The sandbox catches some of these changes when someone explicitly updates it. It misses the ones that happen without triggering an update.

Teams that blame the environment for drift are usually blaming the wrong thing. The environment drifted because nobody updated it. A sandbox does not track production automatically - someone has to make it track production, deliberately, on a schedule tied to something real. Without that, drift is the default outcome.

The better question is not "how do we eliminate the gap" but "which parts of the gap actually cause test failures to miss real production failures." That answer is narrower than most teams assume.

The Part of the Gap That Actually Matters

Not all drift is equal. The sandbox can diverge from production in ways that never cause a test to miss a real failure, and in ways that guarantee it will.

Infrastructure divergence - different instance types, different memory limits, different networking rules - looks significant on paper. Smaller machines, different subnets, scaled-down replicas. In practice, almost none of this changes what an integration test catches. The test is validating how the application handles a payment service response. Whether that test runs on a t3.medium or a production-grade instance does not change whether the response handling is correct.

Behavioral contract drift is the category that actually breaks things. When the order service's simulated payment dependency returns a response structure that no longer matches what the real payment service returns, the tests validate the application against an assumption that production will contradict. The test passes. The integration fails. The sandbox did not fail at its job - the simulation was wrong, and nobody noticed it had become wrong.

Infrastructure parity is satisfying to pursue because progress is measurable. You can diff the configurations, close the gaps, and declare the environments equivalent. Behavioral contract accuracy is harder because it requires ongoing knowledge of what the real upstream service returns right now - not what it returned when the simulation was authored, not what the documentation says it returns, but what the deployed version actually produces today.

Why Simulations Go Stale Faster Than Anyone Expects

When a team first builds a sandbox, the simulated dependencies are accurate. Someone studied what the upstream service actually returns, built a simulation that reflected those observations, and committed it. At that moment, the simulation is correct.

Then the upstream service keeps deploying.

Nobody tells you when the payment service ships a schema change. No notification arrives when a previously optional field becomes required, or when an error format gets restructured, or when a new field appears in the response that your application now needs to handle. The simulation you built against the old version keeps running. The tests keep passing. You deploy. Production encounters the new format on the exact code paths that depend on the fields that changed.

The suite ran clean. Green across the board. And it was wrong - not flaky-wrong, not intermittently-wrong, but systematically wrong in a way that looked identical to correct. That is the more expensive failure mode. A suite that reliably validates against stale assumptions does not look broken. It looks trustworthy right up until production contradicts it.

The teams that manage this best are not the ones that build more accurate simulations initially. They are the ones that connect simulation updates to upstream deployment events rather than to test failures. The trigger determines everything. "Update simulations when tests fail" means the sandbox is wrong from the moment of each upstream deployment until the next failure surfaces the drift - often in production. "Update simulations when upstream services deploy" means the drift window is measured in hours rather than weeks.

Observation-based approaches to generating simulations help here. Tools that capture what upstream services actually return during interactions with staging environments - rather than requiring developers to author what they believe the service returns - start from observed reality rather than from documentation that may have drifted. Keploy, for instance, captures real HTTP traffic at the kernel level through eBPF, which means the simulation reflects what the service actually returned during the recording session rather than what a developer thought it returned. The diff between a previous simulation and an updated one surfaces exactly which fields changed in the upstream response, which is the information the downstream team needs to assess whether application code requires updating alongside the simulation refresh.

The mechanism matters less than the trigger. Simulations updated on upstream deployment events stay accurate. Simulations updated after test failures stay stale.

The Parity You Actually Need

Full production parity is not the goal. Targeted accuracy for the specific behaviors that integration tests are designed to validate is the goal.

The sandbox does not need to replicate production's data volume. It does not need to replicate production's traffic patterns. It does not need to run at production's infrastructure scale. These forms of parity are expensive to maintain and rarely determine whether a test catches a real failure.

What the sandbox needs to do is accurately represent the behavioral contracts between the services being tested - the request and response structures, the error conditions, the state transitions - with enough fidelity that a test failure in the sandbox indicates a real failure that would have occurred in production, and a passing test reflects an integration that will hold.

For sandbox testing to deliver on this, the team needs to be explicit about two things. Which behavioral contracts the sandbox is representing. And how those contracts stay current as upstream services keep evolving.

The first is a design question answered at setup time. The second is a maintenance question that does not have a setup-time answer.

Where "Good Enough" Actually Lives

Spent time on this long enough to have a clear opinion: the teams that get burned are not running bad sandboxes. They are running sandboxes that were accurate once and nobody updated them when upstream services changed.

Get the simulations current. Make sure the test data includes the record shapes that actually exist in production, not just the clean ones from initial setup. That combination catches the integration failures worth catching -- the ones that do not require production to surface them.

It does not catch every failure class. It catches the one that matters most in distributed systems: the assumption about how a dependency behaves that the dependency has since stopped honoring.

The rest of what production reveals - emergent behavior under real load, edge cases in actual user data, failure modes that require realistic traffic patterns to surface - those require production observation to understand. The goal of sandbox testing is not to eliminate that class of learning. It is to eliminate the failures that do not require production to reveal them, cheaply and early.

That is the frame that makes the gap between sandbox and production legible. Not as a problem to solve. As a boundary to understand. The sandbox covers everything inside it. Production reveals what the sandbox structurally cannot cover. Both are doing their jobs. The maintenance work is keeping the sandbox's coverage accurate within its boundary, not expanding the boundary to match production exactly.

Environment drift is not the enemy. Undetected drift in the behavioral contracts that integration tests depend on - going unnoticed until it produces a production failure - is the specific failure mode worth preventing. The distinction is worth making before investing in sandbox infrastructure that aims for parity it can never achieve.

entries.title: Keep calm and call clone with Rust
entries.summary: Ryan sits down with Josh Triplett, member of the Rust Leadership Team at the Rust Project, to chat about how the borrow checker delivers compile-time memory safety without garbage collection overhead, why Rust consistently ranks as developers' most loved language by providing psychological safety for complex systems, and how strict compiler constraints make Rust an ideal target for AI coding agent
entries.content:
Ryan sits down with Josh Triplett, member of the Rust Leadership Team at the Rust Project, to chat about how the borrow checker delivers compile-time memory safety without garbage collection overhead, why Rust consistently ranks as developers' most loved language by providing psychological safety for complex systems, and how strict compiler constraints make Rust an ideal target for AI coding agents.

Rust is an open-source systems programming language focused on performance, type safety, and compile-time memory safety without the runtime overhead of garbage collection.
